strengths: The paper addresses a relevant multilingual NLP problem: producing both reasoning and correct answers in the user's language. Reporting language consistency, accuracy, and their intersection separately makes the competing objectives visible.

The reported improvements in language-consistent accuracy are substantial. On MMATH, the 7B model improves from 17.99% to 62.24% overall LC&Acc, while attaining 99.38% consistency on training languages. PolyMath provides additional evidence across both model sizes.

The reward design and iterative training procedure are clearly presented. The appendices provide the judge prompt, important hyperparameters, and per-language results, and evaluations average four sampling runs.

The ablations provide useful evidence beyond backbone comparisons. Adding CTA to strict language-consistency training improves 1.5B first-iteration accuracy from 35.78% to 39.90% and LC&Acc from 34.43% to 36.88%. The unsuccessful smaller-judge experiment also exposes an important dependency.
weaknesses: The central language-consistency measurement needs validation. Equation (3) treats langdetect outputs as the set of languages present, but probabilistic language candidates do not necessarily identify every language within a mixed-language passage. Segmentation, thresholds, and handling of mathematical or very short answers are unspecified. Because the same detector supplies training rewards and evaluation scores, an independent multilingual audit is needed to substantiate the claim of nearly complete language consistency.

Checkpoint selection leaves evaluation independence unclear. Appendix B.3 reports testing checkpoints every five steps from 320 through 435 for best performance, but identifies no held-out development set or selection criterion. The paper should clarify whether benchmark results influenced selection and report an independently selected evaluation. Four decoding runs do not address training variability, and uncertainty estimates are absent for the smaller ablation gains.

The claim that the method almost overcomes the accuracy–consistency trade-off is stronger than the comparisons support. At iteration 1, 7B accuracy is 58.87%, versus 65.43% for Naive-RL; even iteration 2 reaches only 63.67%. Improving both metrics over an untrained backbone is valuable, but does not establish elimination of the trade-off under comparable training. Baselines receive only first-iteration training, and the soft-consistency baseline uses a single low language-reward weight without a sensitivity study.

Evidence for CTA as a transfer mechanism is limited. Overlap with one English solution can penalize valid alternative derivations, and correct final answers do not guarantee correct reference reasoning. No human validation establishes the judge's alignment accuracy or improved intermediate reasoning. CTA ablations cover only the 1.5B first iteration on MMATH; matched ablations on the final 7B model and PolyMath would strengthen the central methodological claim.

Generalization is uneven and overstated. For 1.5B on MMATH, Arabic consistency falls from 33.31% to 11.03% between iterations, with LC&Acc falling from 6.39% to 2.80%. The language-family explanation rests on only French-versus-Japanese training and does not control other factors. The assertion that related languages must be included is unsupported, and the Chinese-script explanation for Vietnamese is inappropriate for its contemporary Latin writing system.

These are consequential uncertainties about measurement validity and experimental selection, rather than objections based on limited novelty or subjective interest. The large reported gains make this a promising borderline Findings submission, but the current evidence does not yet establish a sufficiently reliable and reproducible positive recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant multilingual NLP problem: producing mathematically correct reasoning and answers in the user's language. Reporting language consistency, accuracy, and their conjunction separately makes the competing objectives visible.

The reported language-consistency gains are substantial across two model sizes and two benchmarks. On MMATH, 7B in-domain LC&Acc improves from 6.89% to 61.66%, while raw accuracy improves from 58.58% to 61.82%. These results support the practical promise of the training approach.

The ablations provide evidence that CTA contributes beyond the strict language reward: for 1.5B Iter-1, adding CTA increases overall accuracy from 35.78% to 39.90% and LC&Acc from 34.43% to 36.88%. Experiments with alternative references and judges provide useful additional observations.
The reward equations, training algorithm, judge prompt, data sources, and many implementation hyperparameters are documented clearly enough to understand the intended method.
weaknesses: The evaluation-selection protocol is insufficiently specified. Appendix B.3 reports testing checkpoints every five steps from 320 to 435 and selecting for best performance, but identifies no separate validation set or selection metric. Decoding temperatures are also chosen for 'best performance' without explaining the tuning split. This leaves an important risk of benchmark-driven selection unresolved. Four evaluation runs provide no reported uncertainty estimates and do not establish robustness across training seeds. The paper also does not document training–benchmark overlap checks.

The central language-consistency measurement needs independent validation. Equation (3) assumes langdetect yields the set of languages actually present in a sequence, but the paper does not specify segmentation, probability thresholds, mathematical-text handling, or how alternative language predictions become this set. Using the same detector for reward and evaluation makes the near-100% result particularly dependent on its validity. A multilingual human audit or independently validated span-level detector is needed to substantiate the claim that complete reasoning traces remain in the requested language.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the advantage of the proposed reward and iterative procedure. SLC-RL uses only one fixed 0.9/0.1 accuracy/language weighting, so its failure does not establish a general limitation of soft rewards. Baselines use the first-iteration training data, whereas the final method receives another training iteration with a longer sequence limit. A matched two-iteration strict-LC baseline without CTA, tuned soft-reward comparisons, and corresponding 7B ablations would make the attribution substantially stronger. PolyMath compares only against the original backbones.

CTA's proposed reasoning-transfer mechanism remains under-validated. The judge measures overlap with one sampled English solution, including its final answer, rather than checking the validity of the target-language reasoning. Correct alternative solutions may receive lower scores, and answer-correct English traces are not necessarily process-correct. No human evaluation establishes that judge scores track reasoning quality. Because CTA is applied only to answer-correct outputs, the accuracy ablation supports its utility as reward shaping but does not by itself demonstrate the claimed transfer of correct reasoning paths.

The claim that the method almost overcomes the consistency–accuracy trade-off is too strong. On MMATH, final 1.5B accuracy is 44.62% versus 50.04% for Naive-RL; for 7B it is 63.67% versus 65.43%. Surpassing DeepSeek-R1-0528 on LC&Acc also does not establish superior mathematical reasoning, since its raw accuracy remains higher. The supported conclusion is a useful operating point with much better language fidelity and a remaining accuracy cost relative to accuracy-only RL.

Generalization conclusions exceed the evidence. For 1.5B, Arabic LC falls from 33.31% to 11.03% between iterations, and adding CTA reduces Arabic LC&Acc from 19.76% to 6.39% in the first-iteration ablation. The language-family explanation rests on just French-only and Japanese-only training, without controlling for initial proficiency or exposure. The discussion of Chinese-derived Vietnamese scripts does not explain results on modern Latin-script Vietnamese. These observations cannot support the prescription that related languages 'must' be included.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant multilingual NLP problem: producing correct mathematical answers with reasoning readable in the user's language. Reporting accuracy, language consistency, and their conjunction makes the intended objective explicit.

The reported improvements are substantial across two model sizes and two benchmarks. On MMATH, 7B joint language consistency and accuracy increases from 17.99% to 62.24%, while accuracy increases from 58.58% to 63.67%. In-domain language consistency exceeds 99% for both final models.

The ablations provide evidence that CTA contributes beyond the strict language reward: adding CTA improves 1.5B first-iteration accuracy from 35.78% to 39.90% and the joint metric from 34.43% to 36.88%. Experiments also examine rejection sampling, cold-start SFT, reference sources, and judge choice.
The reward equations, training algorithm, judge prompt, dataset construction, and many training hyperparameters are provided, making the approach reasonably clear.
weaknesses: The central language-consistency claim lacks independent validation. Training and evaluation use the same langdetect-based criterion, but the implementation of the detected-language set, segmentation, thresholds, and treatment of mathematical notation are unspecified. A language classifier's prediction does not establish that every part of a response uses only that language. Human auditing or an independent detector is needed to substantiate the near-100% claim.

The evaluation protocol leaves a material uncertainty about test-set selection. Appendix B.3 reports evaluating checkpoints every five steps from 320 to 435 for best performance, without identifying a separate development set or selection metric. Training–benchmark overlap checks are also unreported. Four evaluation runs are averaged without uncertainty estimates, limiting confidence in smaller differences.

The evidence does not establish that the accuracy–consistency trade-off is nearly overcome. Naive-RL achieves higher MMATH accuracy than the final models: 50.04% versus 44.62% at 1.5B and 65.43% versus 63.67% at 7B. Joint-metric improvements remain valuable, but comparisons against the untrained backbone cannot isolate the cost of enforcing language consistency. Baselines receive only the first iteration's training data, and the soft reward uses a single weak 0.1 language weight without a strength-matched comparison.

CTA's proposed mechanism is only partially supported. Matching intermediate results to one answer-correct English trace does not establish reasoning validity and can penalize alternative correct solutions. There is no direct validation of judge scores or reasoning quality. CTA ablations cover only the 1.5B first iteration, and the smaller judge performs worse than omitting CTA, suggesting sensitivity that requires further characterization.

Generalization claims need qualification. At 1.5B, Arabic MMATH language consistency falls from 33.31% to 11.03% between iterations; adding CTA also reduces Arabic joint accuracy relative to the no-CTA ablation. The two single-language experiments cannot establish that related languages must be included in training, and the proposed explanation involving Chinese-derived Vietnamese script is not appropriate for modern Vietnamese's Latin writing system.

Overall, the large reported gains make this a close Findings candidate, but the unvalidated central metric and unclear checkpoint-selection protocol prevent a clear soundness recommendation. Resolving these concerns and narrowing the causal claims would materially strengthen the case.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant multilingual NLP problem: producing correct answers while keeping both reasoning and final responses in the user's language. Reporting accuracy, language consistency, and their conjunction makes the practical objective explicit.

The empirical gains in language-consistent correctness are substantial. On MMATH, the 7B model improves LC&Acc from 17.99% to 63.25%, with 98.29% consistency on training languages. Evaluation covers three backbones, ten languages, and two mathematical benchmarks.

The ablations provide useful evidence beyond comparisons with untrained backbones. Removing CTA reduces 1.5B accuracy from 39.90% to 35.78% and LC&Acc from 36.88% to 34.43%. Hard-versus-soft reward comparisons, including a reward-scale control, support the importance of the consistency gate.

The paper supplies reward equations, the judge prompt, training details, and per-language results. Human evaluation on 150 examples reports strong correlations with CTA judgments, providing preliminary validation of the alignment scorer.
weaknesses: The central language-consistency measurement is insufficiently specified and independently validated. Equation 3 treats langdetect as identifying all languages present, but language-classification predictions do not inherently establish the absence of mixed-language spans. Segmentation, probability thresholds, and treatment of formulas and short answers are unspecified. Because the same detector supplies training rewards and evaluation scores, a human audit or independent detector is needed to substantiate the near-100% consistency claim.

Checkpoint selection leaves an important evaluation-integrity question unresolved. Appendix B.3 says checkpoints from steps 320–435 are tested every five steps to select the best performance, without identifying a separate validation set or selection metric. The paper should clarify whether benchmark test results informed selection. Four decoding runs do not address this issue, and no uncertainty estimates or independent training runs are reported.

The accuracy claims are broader than the results support. On MMATH, M-Thinker-4B lowers accuracy from 77.96% to 74.17%; M-Thinker-1.5B Iter-2 remains below Naive-RL, 44.62% versus 50.04%. These results support improved language-consistent correctness and a useful trade-off, rather than uniformly superior reasoning accuracy. The 4B improvement over the strong QRT baseline in LC&Acc is only 72.49% versus 70.68%, without uncertainty estimates.

Evidence attributing gains specifically to reasoning transfer is limited. CTA rewards overlap with one answer-correct English trajectory, which need not itself contain correct intermediate reasoning and can penalize valid alternative solutions. Human agreement validates overlap scoring, not this transfer mechanism. CTA ablations focus on 1.5B Iter-1, while headline results use larger models and additional training. Iter-2 also increases the sequence limit from 16,384 to 24,000 tokens, and comparable two-iteration baselines are absent. PolyMath compares only against original backbones.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The 4B training configuration and judge decoding settings are missing, and Algorithm 1 does not handle an empty set of correct English references. The manuscript's Code/Model/Data labels provide no usable links. Training–benchmark overlap checks and translation-quality validation are also not reported.

The generalization interpretation is overstated. Arabic consistency for 1.5B drops from 33.31% to 11.03% across iterations, demonstrating a substantial exception. Two single-language training experiments cannot establish that related languages must be included in training; the proposed explanation involving Chinese-derived Vietnamese script is inappropriate for modern Vietnamese text. These claims should be framed as tentative observations.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant multilingual NLP problem: producing correct mathematical solutions while keeping both reasoning and answers in the user's language. Reporting accuracy, language consistency, and their intersection separately is useful.

The language-consistency improvements are substantial across three backbones. On MMATH, M-Thinker-7B improves LC&Acc from 17.99% to 63.25%, while accuracy improves from 58.58% to 65.04%. PolyMath provides additional evidence beyond the primary benchmark.

The experiments include useful reward ablations, a reward-magnitude control, alternative judge models, and comparisons with external English references. Human evaluation of 150 examples reports strong correlations with CTA scores, providing some independent support for the alignment judge.
The reward equations, judge prompt, training procedure, and many implementation settings are provided, making the broad approach understandable.
weaknesses: Evaluation independence is insufficiently documented. Appendix B.3 selects the best checkpoint among steps 320–435 at five-step intervals, but identifies no held-out development set or selection metric. If benchmark results guide this selection, reported performance is optimistically biased. The paper also does not document checking overlap between Light-R1 training questions and evaluation problems. These are unresolved protocol concerns, not established evidence of contamination.

The central language-consistency measure needs independent validation. Equation 3 treats langdetect output as the set of languages actually present, without specifying segmentation, confidence thresholds, or handling of mathematical and short answer text. Language-identification candidates need not identify every language appearing in a mixed passage. Using this same detector for training and evaluation leaves the nearly 100% consistency claim insufficiently audited; the human evaluation assesses CTA rather than language consistency.

Claims of simultaneous accuracy improvement are too broad. Qwen3-4B accuracy falls from 77.96% to 74.17%, and M-Thinker-1.5B after two iterations remains below Naive-RL in accuracy (44.62% versus 50.04%). These trade-offs do not negate improvements on the stated joint objective, but require more qualified conclusions. Moreover, two-iteration results receive additional training and a larger sequence limit, whereas RL baselines use the first-iteration setup, preventing attribution of the later gains specifically to the proposed iterative strategy.

Evidence for CTA is promising but narrower than the claimed reasoning-transfer mechanism. The main ablation is confined to 1.5B/Iter-1, where CTA increases accuracy from 35.78% to 39.90% but reduces overall LC from 95.80% to 91.83%. Matching intermediate results from one answer-correct English trace does not establish reasoning correctness and can penalize alternative valid solutions. Human agreement validates this matching judgment, not the causal claim of transferring reasoning ability. No uncertainty estimates or independent training runs establish the reliability of the smaller ablation gains.

Generalization claims overreach the evidence. Arabic LC for the 1.5B model falls from 33.31% to 11.03% between iterations. The French-versus-Japanese experiment cannot isolate language-family effects from script, pretraining coverage, or initial competence, and it does not support the prescription that related languages must be included in training. The explanation invoking Chinese-derived Vietnamese writing is also inappropriate for contemporary Vietnamese text.

Reproduction still requires clarification: Qwen3-4B training settings are omitted from Appendix B.3, and Algorithm 1 samples a correct English reference without checking that the eligible set is nonempty. Together with the checkpoint-selection and detector ambiguities, these gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation despite the substantial empirical signal.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: maintaining the user's language throughout reasoning while preserving answer correctness. Reporting language consistency, accuracy, and their conjunction separately makes the trade-offs visible.

The strongest supported contribution is a substantial improvement in language-consistent correct answers. On MMATH, M-Thinker-7B reaches 63.25% LC&Acc after two iterations, compared with 17.99% for the backbone and 45.01% for SLC-RL. Results across three backbones and additional PolyMath evaluation support the practical utility of the approach.

The ablations provide useful evidence beyond the main comparisons. For 1.5B, adding CTA to hard language enforcement improves accuracy from 35.78% to 39.90% and LC&Acc from 34.43% to 36.88%. The reward-scale control also helps distinguish hard gating from simply increasing the language reward.

The reward equations, training algorithm, judge prompt, data-construction procedure, and substantial implementation details make the central approach understandable and broadly reproducible. Human–judge correlations across five languages provide supporting evidence that CTA measures the intended intermediate-result overlap. Overall, the supported empirical contribution merits Findings.
weaknesses: Claims of broadly improved reasoning accuracy exceed the evidence. M-Thinker-1.5B after two iterations remains below Naive-RL in accuracy (44.62% versus 50.04%), while M-Thinker-4B falls below its original backbone (74.17% versus 77.96%). The contribution is principally a better balance between language fidelity and correctness, rather than uniformly superior reasoning.

The distinctive contribution of CTA is not established consistently across model sizes. Comparing Tables 1 and 10, the 7B first-iteration model improves over hard-LC alone by only 0.04 accuracy points and 0.92 LC&Acc points. Most detailed ablations concern 1.5B. Moreover, intermediate-result overlap with one English solution does not establish reasoning validity and can penalize alternative correct solutions; human agreement validates overlap scoring, not the claimed transfer mechanism.

Evaluation controls limit causal attribution. The two-iteration models receive additional training and a larger sequence-length budget, whereas the principal RL baselines use the first-iteration setting. PolyMath compares against the original backbones rather than the stronger training baselines. Budget-matched iterative baselines would clarify how much improvement comes from the proposed rewards.

The language-consistency measurement needs stronger validation. Training and evaluation use the same langdetect-based criterion, but the paper does not specify sufficiently how its predictions become a set of languages present throughout a response. Whole-sequence language identification does not establish the absence of local code-switching. Independent human or segment-level checks are needed to substantiate the nearly 100% consistency claim.

Several evaluation and reproducibility details remain unclear. Appendix B.3 selects among 24 checkpoints without identifying the held-out selection set; decoding temperatures also differ between trained and untrained methods. Four evaluation runs are averaged without uncertainty estimates or training-seed variation. Qwen3-4B training settings, training–benchmark overlap checks, and handling of an empty correct-English reference set in Algorithm 1 should be specified.

Generalization claims require qualification. For 1.5B, Arabic LC declines from 33.31% to 11.03% between iterations, and overall OOD LC also decreases. The language-family explanation rests on only two single-language training experiments and does not separate genealogy, script, and pretraining exposure. The assertion that related languages must be included in training is not supported by this evidence.
